Partial\\n            result = \\\"pass\\\"\\n            reason = \\\"Used only one required tool\\\"\\n        else:\\n            score = 1.0  # Poor\\n            result = \\\"fail\\\"\\n            reason = \\\"No relevant tools used\\\"\\n        \\n        return {\\n            \\\"tool_call_accuracy\\\": score,\\n            \\\"tool_call_accuracy_result\\\": result,\\n            \\\"tool_call_accuracy_threshold\\\": 3.0,\\n            \\\"tool_call_accuracy_reason\\\": reason\\n        }\\n\\nclass CoordinationEfficiencyEvaluator:\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Evaluates how efficiently the agent coordinates weather and time tools.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    \\n    def __init__(self):\\n        pass\\n    \\n    def __call__(self, *, query: str, tool_calls: List[Dict], **kwargs) -> Dict[str, Union[str, float]]:\\n        \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n        Evaluate coordination efficiency based on:\\n        - Whether both weather and time tools are used when both are needed\\n        - Whether tools are called in parallel vs sequential (parallel is better)\\n        - Whether excessive/unnecessary tool calls are made\\n        \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n        if not tool_calls:\\n            return {\\n                \\\"coordination_efficiency\\\": \\\"not_applicable\\\",\\n                \\\"coordination_efficiency_score\\\": 0.0,\\n                \\\"coordination_efficiency_reason\\\": \\\"No tool calls found\\\"\\n            }\\n        \\n        # Parse query to determine if both weather and time are requested\\n        query_lower = query.lower()\\n        needs_weather = any(word in query_lower for word in ['weather', 'temperature', 'sunny', 'rain', 'climate'])\\n        needs_time = any(word in query_lower for word in ['time', 'utc', 'clock', 'hour', 'minute', 'when'])\\n        \\n        if not (needs_weather and needs_time):\\n            return {\\n                \\\"coordination_efficiency\\\": \\\"not_applicable\\\", \\n                \\\"coordination_efficiency_score\\\": 0.0,\\n                \\\"coordination_efficiency_reason\\\": \\\"Query does not require both weather and time\\\"\\n            }\\n        \\n        # Extract tool names from tool calls\\n        weather_tools = []\\n        time_tools = []\\n        other_tools = []\\n        \\n        for call in tool_calls:\\n            if isinstance(call, dict):\\n                name = call.get('name', '')\\n                if 'weather' in name.lower():\\n                    weather_tools.append(call)\\n                elif 'time' in name.lower():\\n                    time_tools.append(call)\\n                else:\\n                    other_tools.append(call)\\n        \\n        has_weather_call = len(weather_tools) > 0\\n        has_time_call = len(time_tools) > 0\\n        total_calls = len(tool_calls)\\n        \\n        # Score based on coordination quality\\n        score = 0.0\\n        reason_parts = []\\n        \\n        if has_weather_call and has_time_call:\\n            score += 3.0  # Base score for using both required tools\\n            reason_parts.append(\\\"Used both weather and time tools\\\")\\n            \\n            # Check for parallel execution (tools called in same LLM turn)\\n            if len(tool_calls) == 2:  # Optimal case: exactly 2 calls\\n                score += 2.0\\n                reason_parts.append(\\\"Optimal parallel execution\\\")\\n            elif len(tool_calls) > 2:\\n                score += 1.0  # Some points for parallel but with extra calls\\n                reason_parts.append(\\\"Parallel execution with extra calls\\\")\\n            else:\\n                reason_parts.append(\\\"Sequential execution\\\")\\n        elif has_weather_call or has_time_call:\\n            score += 1.0  # Partial score for using one required tool\\n            missing = \\\"time\\\" if has_weather_call else \\\"weather\\\"\\n            reason_parts.append(f\\\"Missing {missing} tool call\\\")\\n        else:\\n            reason_parts.append(\\\"Missing both required tool calls\\\")\\n        \\n        # Efficiency rating\\n        if score >= 4.5:\\n            efficiency = \\\"excellent\\\"\\n        elif score >= 3.0:\\n            efficiency = \\\"good\\\"\\n        elif score >= 1.5:\\n            efficiency = \\\"fair\\\"\\n        else:\\n            efficiency = \\\"poor\\\"\\n        \\n        return {\\n            \\\"coordination_efficiency\\\": efficiency,\\n            \\\"coordination_efficiency_score\\\": score,\\n            \\\"coordination_efficiency_reason\\\": \\\"; \\\".join(reason_parts)\\n        }\\n\\n\\nclass ResponseCompletenessEvaluator:\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Evaluates whether the response includes both weather and time information when both are requested.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    \\n    def __init__(self):\\n        pass\\n    \\n    def __call__(self, *, query: str, response: str, **kwargs) -> Dict[str, Union[str, float]]:\\n        \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n        Evaluate response completeness for weather-time coordination queries.\\n        \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n        query_lower = query.lower()\\n        response_lower = response.lower()\\n        \\n        # Check if query requests both weather and time\\n        needs_weather = any(word in query_lower for word in ['weather', 'temperature', 'sunny', 'rain', 'climate'])\\n        needs_time = any(word in query_lower for word in ['time', 'utc', 'clock', 'hour', 'minute', 'when'])\\n        \\n        if not (needs_weather and needs_time):\\n            return {\\n                \\\"response_completeness\\\": \\\"not_applicable\\\",\\n                \\\"response_completeness_score\\\": 0.0,\\n                \\\"response_completeness_reason\\\": \\\"Query does not require both weather and time\\\"\\n            }\\n        \\n        # Check if response contains weather information\\n        has_weather_info = any(word in response_lower for word in [\\n            'weather', 'temperature', 'sunny', 'rain', 'cloudy', 'degrees', '°c', '°f', 'celsius', 'fahrenheit'\\n        ])\\n        \\n        # Check if response contains time information\\n        has_time_info = any(word in response_lower for word in [\\n            'time', 'utc', 'am', 'pm', 'hour', 'minute', 'clock', ':', 'september', 'monday', 'tuesday'\\n        ]) or any(char.isdigit() and ':' in response for char in response)\\n        \\n        score = 0.0\\n        reason_parts = []\\n        \\n        if has_weather_info and has_time_info:\\n            score = 5.0\\n            completeness = \\\"complete\\\"\\n            reason_parts.append(\\\"Contains both weather and time information\\\")\\n        elif has_weather_info or has_time_info:\\n            score = 2.5\\n            completeness = \\\"partial\\\"\\n            missing = \\\"time\\\" if has_weather_info else \\\"weather\\\"\\n            reason_parts.append(f\\\"Contains only {missing} information\\\")\\n        else:\\n            score = 0.0\\n            completeness = \\\"incomplete\\\"\\n            reason_parts.append(\\\"Missing both weather and time information\\\")\\n        \\n        return {\\n            \\\"response_completeness\\\": completeness,\\n            \\\"response_completeness_score\\\": score,\\n            \\\"response_completeness_reason\\\": \\\"; \\\".join(reason_parts)\\n        }\\n\\n\\ndef convert_traces_to_evaluation_data(traces_file: str) -> List[Dict]:\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    Convert OpenTelemetry traces to evaluation data format.\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    with open(traces_file, 'r') as f:\\n        data = json.load(f)\\n    \\n    evaluation_data = []\\n    \\n    for trace in data.get('traces', []):\\n        # Extract query from user message event\\n        query = None\\n        response = None\\n        tool_calls = []\\n        \\n        for event in trace.get('events', []):\\n            if event['name'] == 'gen_ai.user.message':\\n                body = json.loads(event['body'])\\n                contents = body.get('contents', [])\\n                if contents and contents[0].get('type') == 'text':\\n                    query = contents[0]['text']\\n            \\n            elif event['name'] == 'gen_ai.choice':\\n                body = json.loads(event['body'])\\n                message = body.get('message', {})\\n                contents = message.get('contents', [])\\n                \\n                for content in contents:\\n                    if content.get('type') == 'function_call':\\n                        # Convert to tool call format expected by evaluator\\n                        tool_call = {\\n                            \\\"type\\\": \\\"tool_call\\\",\\n                            \\\"tool_call_id\\\": content.get('call_id', ''),\\n                            \\\"name\\\": content.get('name', ''),\\n                            \\\"arguments\\\": json.loads(content.get('arguments', '{}'))\\n                        }\\n                        tool_calls.append(tool_call)\\n                    \\n                    elif content.get('type') == 'text':\\n                        response = content.get('text', '')\\n        \\n        if query:\\n            # ✅ **If available**: Use the built-in evaluator\r\n   - ❌ **If not available**: Proceed to step 2\r\n\r\n2. **Determine Custom Evaluator Type**: If no built-in evaluator meets your needs, choose the appropriate custom implementation:\r\n   - Your dataset must include all required fields for your chosen evaluators:\r\n    - **Format**: JSONL (JSON Lines) - each line is a separate JSON object\r\n    - **DO NOT INCLUDE TIMESTAMPS IN YOUR DATASET**: Fields with timestamp values (e.g., `2025-08-25T11:27:49.437767`) will cause SDK errors\r\n    - **Include required columns**: Ensure all columns needed by your evaluators are present\r\n    - **Consistent naming**: Use column mapping in evaluator_config to map your data fields to evaluator parameters. Use `${data.column_name}` to refer the column in dataset\r\n- Set `output_path` to make sure evaluation results is saved\r\n- Results will include:\r\n  - **Row-level evaluation data**: Individual scores and reasons for each data point\r\n  - **Aggregate metrics**: Summary statistics across all evaluated data **automatically computed by the API**\r\n  - **Per-evaluator metrics**: Detailed performance metrics for each evaluator **with built-in aggregation**\r\n\r\n## Complete Example: Combining Three Types of Evaluators\r\n\r\nHere's a complete example combining built-in evaluator, custom code-based evaluator and custom prompt-based evaluator:\r\n\r\n```python\r\nfrom azure.ai.evaluation import evaluate, TaskAdherenceEvaluator, OpenAIModelConfiguration\r\nimport os\r\nimport json\r\nfrom promptflow.client import load_flow # used by custom prompt-based evaluators\r\n\r\n# 1. Define custom prompt-based evaluators\r\nclass FriendlinessEvaluator:\r\n    def __init__(self, model_config):\r\n        self._flow = load_flow(source=\"friendliness.prompty\", model={\"configuration\": model_config})\r\n\r\n    def __call__(self, *, response: str, **kwargs):\r\n        llm_response = self._flow(response=response)\r\n        try:\r\n            response = json.loads(llm_response)\r\n        except Exception as ex:\r\n            response = llm_response\r\n        return response\r\n\r\n# 4. Run evaluation\r\nresult = evaluate(\r\n    data=\"your_data.jsonl\",\r\n    evaluators={\r\n        \"task_adherence\": task_adherence_evaluator,\r\n        \"answer_length\": answer_length_evaluator,\r\n        \"friendliness\": friendliness_evaluator\r\n    },\r\n    evaluator_config={\r\n        \"task_adherence\": {\r\n            \"column_mapping\": {\r\n                \"query\": \"${data.query}\",\r\n                \"response\": \"${data.response}\"\r\n            }\r\n        },\r\n        \"answer_length\": {\r\n            \"column_mapping\": {\r\n                \"answer\": \"${data.response}\"\r\n            }\r\n        },\r\n        \"friendliness\": {\r\n            \"response\": \"${data.response}\"\r\n        }\r\n    }\r\n)\r\n```"

A good plan should break the task into meaningful, logically ordered steps that are easy to verify as you go. Note that plans are not for padding out simple work with filler steps or stating the obvious. \nUse this tool to create and manage a structured todo list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.\nIt also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.\n\nNOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. Never start work with zero `in-progress` items.\n- Keep only one todo `in-progress` at a time. Do not leave completion implicit.\n- Before ending your turn or declaring completion: ensure EVERY todo is explicitly marked (`not-started`, `in-progress`, or `completed`). If the work is finished, ALL todos must be marked `completed`. Your dataset must include all required fields for your chosen evaluators:\r\n    - **Format**: JSONL (JSON Lines) - each line is a separate JSON object\r\n    - **DO NOT INCLUDE TIMESTAMPS IN YOUR DATASET**: Fields with timestamp values (e.g., `2025-08-25T11:27:49.437767`) will cause SDK errors\r\n    - **Include required columns**: Ensure all columns needed by your evaluators are present\r\n    - **Consistent naming**: Use column mapping in evaluator_config to map your data fields to evaluator parameters. Use `${data.column_name}` to refer the column in dataset\r\n- Set `output_path` to make sure evaluation results is saved\r\n- Results will include:\r\n  - **Row-level evaluation data**: Individual scores and reasons for each data point\r\n  - **Aggregate metrics**: Summary statistics across all evaluated data **automatically computed by the API**\r\n  - **Per-evaluator metrics**: Detailed performance metrics for each evaluator **with built-in aggregation**\r\n\r\n## Complete Example: Combining Three Types of Evaluators\r\n\r\nHere's a complete example combining built-in evaluator, custom code-based evaluator and custom prompt-based evaluator:\r\n\r\n```python\r\nfrom azure.ai.evaluation import evaluate, TaskAdherenceEvaluator, OpenAIModelConfiguration\r\nimport os\r\nimport json\r\nfrom promptflow.client import load_flow # used by custom prompt-based evaluators\r\n\r\n# 1. Define custom prompt-based evaluators\r\nclass FriendlinessEvaluator:\r\n    def __init__(self, model_config):\r\n        self._flow = load_flow(source=\"friendliness.prompty\", model={\"configuration\": model_config})\r\n\r\n    def __call__(self, *, response: str, **kwargs):\r\n        llm_response = self._flow(response=response)\r\n        try:\r\n            response = json.loads(llm_response)\r\n        except Exception as ex:\r\n            response = llm_response\r\n        return response\r\n\r\n# 4. ✅ **If available**: Use the built-in evaluator\r\n   - ❌ **If not available**: Proceed to step 2\r\n\r\n2. **Determine Custom Evaluator Type**: If no built-in evaluator meets your needs, choose the appropriate custom implementation:\r\n   - **Code-based Evaluator**: For objective, measurable criteria that require specific business logic\r\n   - **Prompt-based Evaluator**: For subjective criteria requiring human-like judgment that an LLM can assess\r\n\r\n#### Option A: Built-in Evaluators (⭐ Start Here First)\r\n\r\nBuilt-in evaluators are pre-implemented and ready to use. They follow the same `__init__` and `__call__` pattern internally. **Always check these first** before implementing custom evaluators.\r\n\r\n**⭐ Available Built-in Evaluators for AI Features:** Use the **github_repo** tool to search the `Azure/azure-sdk-for-python` repository for `_evaluators` to understand the built-in evaluators.\r\n\r\n#### Option B: Custom Code-based Evaluators\r\n\r\nUse the **github_repo** tool to search the `MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs` repository for \"custom code-based evaluators\" to understand custom code-based evaluators.\r\n\r\n#### Option C: Custom Prompt-based Evaluators (LLM as Judge)\r\n\r\nUse the **github_repo** tool to search the `MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs` repository for \"custom prompt-based evaluators\" to understand custom prompt-based evaluators.\r\n\r\n### Set Model Configuration\r\n\r\n**🔍 First: Use github_repo tool** to search the `Azure/azure-sdk-for-python` repository for `OpenAIModelConfiguration` and `AzureOpenAIModelConfiguration` to understand configuration patterns and examples.\r\n\r\nFor built-in evaluators that need model configuration and for custom prompt-based evaluators, you need to set model configuration (`OpenAIModelConfiguration`, `AzureOpenAIModelConfiguration`):\r\n- Get AI model guidance to determine the most suitable model, use \"GitHub\" and \"AzureAIFoundry\" as preferred host\r\n- For getting started, consider GitHub models with Free-tier endpoint\r\n\r\nFor example:\r\n```python\r\nfrom azure.ai.evaluation import OpenAIModelConfiguration\r\nmodel_config = OpenAIModelConfiguration(\r\n    type=\"openai\", # Your dataset must include all required fields for your chosen evaluators:\r\n    - **Format**: JSONL (JSON Lines) - each line is a separate JSON object\r\n    - **DO NOT INCLUDE TIMESTAMPS IN YOUR DATASET**: Fields with timestamp values (e.g., `2025-08-25T11:27:49.437767`) will cause SDK errors\r\n    - **Include required columns**: Ensure all columns needed by your evaluators are present\r\n    - **Consistent naming**: Use column mapping in evaluator_config to map your data fields to evaluator parameters. Use `${data.column_name}` to refer the column in dataset\r\n- Set `output_path` to make sure evaluation results is saved\r\n- Results will include:\r\n  - **Row-level evaluation data**: Individual scores and reasons for each data point\r\n  - **Aggregate metrics**: Summary statistics across all evaluated data **automatically computed by the API**\r\n  - **Per-evaluator metrics**: Detailed performance metrics for each evaluator **with built-in aggregation**\r\n\r\n## Complete Example: Combining Three Types of Evaluators\r\n\r\nHere's a complete example combining built-in evaluator, custom code-based evaluator and custom prompt-based evaluator:\r\n\r\n```python\r\nfrom azure.ai.evaluation import evaluate, TaskAdherenceEvaluator, OpenAIModelConfiguration\r\nimport os\r\nimport json\r\nfrom promptflow.client import load_flow # used by custom prompt-based evaluators\r\n\r\n# 1. ✅ **If available**: Use the built-in evaluator\r\n   - ❌ **If not available**: Proceed to step 2\r\n\r\n2. **Determine Custom Evaluator Type**: If no built-in evaluator meets your needs, choose the appropriate custom implementation:\r\n   - **Code-based Evaluator**: For objective, measurable criteria that require specific business logic\r\n   - **Prompt-based Evaluator**: For subjective criteria requiring human-like judgment that an LLM can assess\r\n\r\n#### Option A: Built-in Evaluators (⭐ Start Here First)\r\n\r\nBuilt-in evaluators are pre-implemented and ready to use. They follow the same `__init__` and `__call__` pattern internally. **Always check these first** before implementing custom evaluators.\r\n\r\n**⭐ Available Built-in Evaluators for AI Features:** Use the **github_repo** tool to search the `Azure/azure-sdk-for-python` repository for `_evaluators` to understand the built-in evaluators.\r\n\r\n#### Option B: Custom Code-based Evaluators\r\n\r\nUse the **github_repo** tool to search the `MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs` repository for \"custom code-based evaluators\" to understand custom code-based evaluators.\r\n\r\n#### Option C: Custom Prompt-based Evaluators (LLM as Judge)\r\n\r\nUse the **github_repo** tool to search the `MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs` repository for \"custom prompt-based evaluators\" to understand custom prompt-based evaluators.\r\n\r\n### Set Model Configuration\r\n\r\n**🔍 First: Use github_repo tool** to search the `Azure/azure-sdk-for-python` repository for `OpenAIModelConfiguration` and `AzureOpenAIModelConfiguration` to understand configuration patterns and examples.\r\n\r\nFor built-in evaluators that need model configuration and for custom prompt-based evaluators, you need to set model configuration (`OpenAIModelConfiguration`, `AzureOpenAIModelConfiguration`):\r\n- Get AI model guidance to determine the most suitable model, use \"GitHub\" and \"AzureAIFoundry\" as preferred host\r\n- For getting started, consider GitHub models with Free-tier endpoint\r\n\r\nFor example:\r\n```python\r\nfrom azure.ai.evaluation import OpenAIModelConfiguration\r\nmodel_config = OpenAIModelConfiguration(\r\n    type=\"openai\", # Your dataset must include all required fields for your chosen evaluators:\r\n    - **Format**: JSONL (JSON Lines) - each line is a separate JSON object\r\n    - **DO NOT INCLUDE TIMESTAMPS IN YOUR DATASET**: Fields with timestamp values (e.g., `2025-08-25T11:27:49.437767`) will cause SDK errors\r\n    - **Include required columns**: Ensure all columns needed by your evaluators are present\r\n    - **Consistent naming**: Use column mapping in evaluator_config to map your data fields to evaluator parameters. Use `${data.column_name}` to refer the column in dataset\r\n- Set `output_path` to make sure evaluation results is saved\r\n- Results will include:\r\n  - **Row-level evaluation data**: Individual scores and reasons for each data point\r\n  - **Aggregate metrics**: Summary statistics across all evaluated data **automatically computed by the API**\r\n  - **Per-evaluator metrics**: Detailed performance metrics for each evaluator **with built-in aggregation**\r\n\r\n## Complete Example: Combining Three Types of Evaluators\r\n\r\nHere's a complete example combining built-in evaluator, custom code-based evaluator and custom prompt-based evaluator:\r\n\r\n```python\r\nfrom azure.ai.evaluation import evaluate, TaskAdherenceEvaluator, OpenAIModelConfiguration\r\nimport os\r\nimport json\r\nfrom promptflow.client import load_flow # used by custom prompt-based evaluators\r\n\r\n# 1. Define custom prompt-based evaluators\r\nclass FriendlinessEvaluator:\r\n    def __init__(self, model_config):\r\n        self._flow = load_flow(source=\"friendliness.prompty\", model={\"configuration\": model_config})\r\n\r\n    def __call__(self, *, response: str, **kwargs):\r\n        llm_response = self._flow(response=response)\r\n        try:\r\n            response = json.loads(llm_response)\r\n        except Exception as ex:\r\n            response = llm_response\r\n        return response\r\n\r\n# 4.
